newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire peace talks in shaky start, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire peace talks in shaky start, rebels advance.

text.p: Zaire's peace process got off to a shaky start in South Africa on Saturday as rebels overran another key city in Zaire and negotiators apparently failed to start substantive negotiations.

The rebels also bristled at charges they had refused to let international relief agencies help about 100,000 Rwandan refugees on territory they control and gave authorisation to the United Nations to begin a massive -- and expensive -- airlift.
And at his Goma headquarters, rebel leader Laurent Kabila rubbed salt in government wounds by taking a march-past by 400 re-educated former government soldiers.
In Pretoria, Zaire government representatives met rebel envoys at a formal ceremony in the South African government cabinet chambers.
After short speeches, there was an icy handshake between Zairean foreign minister Kamanda wa Kamanda and Bizima Karaha of the rebel Alliance.
The negotiators parted and were later moved to a secret location outside Pretoria to get down to business. But by nightfall there was no word on talks starting.
Karaha told Reuters he had reached the proposed site of their talks, but there had been no meeting yet.
"I won't speculate. I simply do not know," he said. "We may start talking tonight, or it may not be until tomorrow. I cannot tell you because I do not know."
He declined to say where he was telephoning from.
Asked earlier about the apparent delay, a spokesman for the Zaire government side said: "We told you. Today was just the opening. The talks begin tomorrow."

Any hope of a quick ceasefire accord to get the talks going was buried by news the advancing rebels had captured the central Zaire city of Mbuji-Mayi, heart of the diamond-mining region, to be greeted with cheers from residents.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) is bent on toppling President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has ruled for 31 years, and arrived in South Africa clearly prepared to negotiate from a position of strength.
The rebels are now expected to turn their guns in the direction of Zaire's second largest city, Lubumbashi, where they may be welcomed with open arms as in their earlier conquests.
In a blunt opening speech Karaha underlined the widespread view that it was rebel victories and Kabila's mounting popularity that had driven the government into negotiations.
"We are here because those brothers of ours have realised for the first time they can't make it with mercenaries and genociders. They can only make it with us if they still want to survive," he said.

Within government ranks, the personal power of the ailing Mobutu was diluted: Kinshasa's negotiating team included a government under the leadership of his arch-rival, Etienne Tshisekedi, as well as opposition party members.
The Kinshasa envoys stared stonily ahead as Karaha pledged Zaire would be "free of misery, disease and dictatorship".
The opening gambits appeared to offer scant hope of rapid progress towards a ceasefire in the war.
"I know we should have no illusions as to the ability of such meetings to produce spectacular results," U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said. "But we shall leave no stone unturned."
Karaha said taking towns was not important.
"The whole country should be liberated," he said. "Mobutu has to go."
